## Standing directives

- **DIRCP01-1** · In each Part 3, take at least one causal chain from an earlier memorandum whose later links fall in a phase this memorandum revises, and test it against the war as now written; where the new provision or free play makes it resolve differently, say so in the chain review and let it (every chain in memoranda 001–005 resolved as predicted, which is more likely tidiness than foresight)
- **DIRCP01-2** · A war-wide figure for lives saved, or any war-wide count built from a rate, must be shown at work in at least two dated events in the chapters before a later memorandum repeats it; until then it is cited as a judgment resting on its rate, with the rate named (CP01 calibration of the [X-004] lives-saved figure)
- **DIRMT01-1** · In every §4.N, state the date of the Republic's fall as its own estimate, separately from the rung: a window, the mechanisms in the cumulative force that pull it earlier and those that pull it later, and which dominate and why; "on the historical timeline" may be written only as the conclusion of that test, and a change of date is reported as a change of date and does not by itself move the rung between (a) and (b) while the ladder's overlap stands (the historical fall, twenty-five months after the last American combat troops left, satisfies the words of rung (b), and seven memoranda have kept (a) and (b) apart by the date alone)
- **DIRMT01-2** · In every §4.N, carry a running sum of the sub-band estimates that all memoranda so far have made on the same variable (American dead, ARVN battalions not lost, and the like), tagged as exercise judgments with their rates named, and say whether the sum crosses a band; and treat the American aid appropriation of 1974 and the refusal of April 1975 as events a provision can change, not as history to be carried (each memorandum judged its own saving of American lives alone, and the 1974 vote was never examined)
- **DIRMT01-3** · Where a chapter's end vector returns a variable to the historical state from a non-zero band in the phase before, the chapter must contain the dated events that produce the convergence; and in every memorandum that revises Phase VI, state in the phase's analysis the Republic's state at the end of 1974, before the last offensive, because the phase's end vector is measured after the fall and cannot record anything the fall erased (Phase V returned four countryside variables to history with no sentence on the countryside, and Phase VI's vector is blind by construction)
- **DIRMT01-4** · Where a memorandum alters an event and keeps its historical outcome, name what absorbs the difference (the enemy's choice to bypass or decline, a decision above the level the provision reached, an external fixed by law or by another government) and show it in the event; "as historically" is a conclusion, never a mechanism (in Phase VI at least six altered events in the last campaign restore the historical outcome by statement)
- **DIRMT01-5** · Where a perverse effect or a capture undoes a gain, state the net in both directions with its weight, and where several provisions' institutions fall to the same mechanism in the same years, judge them together before judging each alone (four institutions from four memoranda fall to the lapse of the American lever in 1970–71, each judged alone, and every memorandum closes on the gain undone)
- **DIRMT01-6** · The next memorandum or review whose Part 3 revises Phase V or VI states the PAVN's 1972 losses in this war against the historical figure and the rebuilding time that follows, before writing 1973–75 (memorandum 005 made the measured sieges the enemy's worst battles; Phase V keeps the historical losses and Phase VI the historical rebuilding)
- **DIRMT01-7** · Every memorandum whose Part 3 revises Phase V or VI tests its effects against the critical path of 1975 (the palace's orders of 13–14 March, the 1st Corps' march against the rains, and Minh's surrender) and states whether any mechanism could delay the collapse of I and II Corps by about three weeks, the threshold beyond which the assault falls into the rains; effects on fights the PAVN could bypass are reported as such (the date of the fall was carried for seven memoranda without its critical path ever being stated)
- **DIRMT01-8** · Every memorandum touching the countryside states its effect separately for the Delta, the coastal lowlands of I and II Corps, the Highlands and their peoples, and the Saigon belt, and names a place in each where the effect is shown or says why there is none (the Delta was written as a footnote, the Montagnards appear twice and FULRO never, and Binh Dinh vanished from the record after 1967)
- **DIRMT01-9** · Every provision touching the reliability of the ARVN or the territorial forces addresses the soldier's family: where it lives, what his pay buys after inflation, and what happens to it when the unit moves or the front gives way (the corps of 1975 dissolved toward their families, and no memorandum had treated them)
- **DIRMT01-10** · The enemy's decisions have authors: in each memorandum name the body or commander who took the enemy's decision of G3, and distinguish Hanoi, the B-2 Front and COSVN, and the regional fronts where they differed; treat the Soviet and Chinese supply as variables with their own politics (COSVN vanishes from the record after 1971, the Phuoc Long argument is told as one mind, and the Soviet deliveries of 1974 are absent)
- **DIRMT01-11** · Every memorandum touching the countryside or the RVNAF states its effect on rice (production, procurement and the Front's take) and on the piaster and the soldier's pay, with at least one dated event (rice appears eleven times in Phase II and once in 1972–75, the years the economy decided)
- **DIRCP02-1** · At each checkpoint, consolidate a chapter over the limit in two steps: first merge minor historical events into summary events, then merge each memorandum's own minor NEW events in that phase into one summary per memorandum, keeping every fact a later memorandum or position cites by event number; and every memorandum's §4 adds to a phase's overview and ending only one paragraph, replacing rather than appending where an earlier memorandum's paragraph states the same variable (CP02 consolidation of P1 and P2, still about 7,600 and 9,300 words over the limit after the first step)
- **DIRCP02-2** · In each Part 3 the chain taken under DIRCP01-1 must be one written by another memorandum whose terminal event this memorandum did not write; C006-4, whose terminal link no chapter carries, is the first such chain for any memorandum revising Phase V (17 of 19 chains in memoranda 006–010 resolved as their authors predicted)
- **DIRCP02-3** · Where a provision acts on a variable already at the cap of the bands in a phase, the memorandum states its increment in the running sum of DIRMT01-2 with the factors it multiplies and how they overlap, and names the target the enemy moves to in answer (POSCP02-2); a product of overlapping judgments is reported as a range with its upper bound marked (CP02 calibration of the battalions-not-broken figure)
- **DIRR01-1** · DIRCP02-3's rule for a variable "already at the cap of the bands" lapses, because the scale has no cap short of a different war: a provision that acts on such a variable re-judges its range, and the range of the facet it acts on, and the running sums of DIRMT01-2 now say which part of that range they support rather than whether they cross a band; the rest of DIRCP02-3 stands, the target the enemy moves to in answer is still named, and a product of overlapping judgments is still reported as a range with its upper bound marked (the user's change of scale, 24 Nov 2026; R01)
- **DIRR01-2** · A range marked "converted" is the old band restated, not a judgment: it is never cited as a judgment of the war, and every memorandum or checkpoint whose evidence bears on a converted entry, or on one of the four entries converted from the cap, re-judges it with a confidence and a note (R01's mechanical conversion of the end vectors)
- **DIRR01-3** · Where a variable has facets, §2 names the facet a provision acts on, and every revised phase that judges a facet names the parent's binding facet and says why it binds; the parent is never the average of its facets, and a gain on one facet is not reported as a gain on the parent unless the binding facet moved (the user's point of 24 Nov 2026 that "ARVN effectiveness" does not discriminate between urban combat, combined arms, anti-armor and the rest)
- **DIRR02-1** · A study describes the war and never changes it: no study adds, alters or cancels an event or moves the end state, and where a study finds the record inconsistent it records a question for an erratum or a checkpoint rather than settling it (the user's design of 24 Nov 2026; R02)
- **DIRR02-2** · Every memorandum whose variables a study covers is written against that study: Part 2 judges its pushes against the study's values and says plainly when the provision's effect contradicts the study and which should give way, and Part 3 records what changed in the area in the study's entry (R02)
- **DIRR02-3** · A study's value is never cited as a measurement: study values are exercise judgments on the R01 scale, an indicator a study gives carries its own provenance, and a figure the study generates carries the X-tag of its study run (X-ST01 and so on) forever (A13a; R02)

# Card 012 — Combined US–RVN–ROK–Australian operations command; combined interagency task force against the VCI

*Memorandum 012 · status part1 · full record: memos/012/ · generated by fie.py*

## P012a · Combined Operations Command, Vietnam: a combined US, Republic of Vietnam, Republic of Korea and Australian operations command under COMUSMACV as combined commander, with Vietnamese, Korean and Australian deputies and an integrated combined staff on the 2026 model of the ROK–US Combined Forces Command and the coalition joint headquarters, holding operational control of the ARVN corps and their divisions, the ROK forces in Vietnam and the Australian task force, the national chains keeping administration, discipline and the right of appeal to their governments
One combined headquarters in Saigon and four combined corps-area operations centres [U: the user's default: COMUSMACV commands, RVNAF, ROK and Australian forces under its operational control]; command and staff only, the allied contingents at their historical size and timing [U] · spaces ~700–1,000 US personnel, of whom ~600–900 military spaces [E: an integrated combined staff of about 1,400–2,000 at the headquarters and the four corps-area centres, about half American, against the historical MACV staff, which the combined staff absorbs in part]; no troop ceiling is set (CONFIG) · arrives 1964-01-01 · FIX, STRIKE, SECURE, ADVISE, SUSTAIN, FIND · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Historical: Westmoreland's April 1965 combined-headquarters proposal withdrawn after Vietnamese "extreme sensitivity"; sovereignty and the colonialism charge the obstacles [M012·S1]
- Historical: ROK never under US operational control; working arrangement of 6 September 1965 [M012·S2]; "cooperative and coordinative" relations [M012·S3]; ROK Army 49,755 in 1969 [M012·S4]
- Historical: 1 ATF under OPCON of II FFV with its own area in Phuoc Tuy; 7,672 Australians at the February 1968 peak [M012·S5]
- Model: ROK–US Combined Forces Command, 7 November 1978; American commander, Korean deputy, alternating staff leads [M012·S6]
- Combined staff ~1,400–2,000, of whom ~700–1,000 American, ~500–750 Vietnamese, ~110–200 Korean, ~40–80 Australian; ~250–400 interpreters [E: D2]
- US spaces ~600–900 military, net new ~300–500 after MACV growth absorbed; no ceiling (CONFIG) [E: judgment from the period's establishments and practice]
- Tasking an ARVN division: ~24–48 hours in the corps area against several days historically [E: D5]
- Fire coordination: ARVN call to fire ~⅓–½ faster where US guns are present [E: judgment from the period's establishments and practice]
- Vietnamese staff-trained field-grade officers: ~200–300 in 1964, ~600–900 by 1968 — the rate limit [E: memorandum 007's staff-college output]
- Cost: ~$40–70 million a year running, ~$15–25 million construction [E: 1964 prices]

**Negative specification.** - **It adds no troops.** It is a command and staff only. The Korean and Australian contingents arrive at their historical size and timing [U].
- **It does not make ARVN commanders good.** An order reaches a commander who will obey it, half obey it or report it obeyed. Relief goes through the national chain and takes weeks.
- **It does not command the territorial forces, the province chiefs or the police.** It reaches the hamlets only through the corps. It has nothing to say about who holds a hamlet at night.
- **It does not command the Koreans beyond what Seoul allows.** Each nation keeps a red card on employment, and Korean caution about casualties is national policy, not a staff problem.
- **It does not find the main force.** It acts faster and across boundaries on what something else finds; it sees nothing under canopy or at night (A6).
- **It does not change the constraints.** The sanctuaries, the DMZ and the rules of engagement are as CONFIG sets them.
- **It does not keep its plans secret.** Every combined plan is in Vietnamese hands from its first draft, and the enemy has agents among them.
- **It does not stop coups.** A junta that falls takes its consent to operational control with it.
- **It does not survive withdrawal unchanged.** It can be handed to a Vietnamese commander. The American fires it exists to allocate cannot.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy the seams: the corps boundary where the ARVN and the Americans each assumed the other was responsible, the edge of the Korean area on the II Corps coast, and the days of negotiation before an ARVN division moved to block a regiment's withdrawal. It denies him the ARVN commander's private veto on battle, wherever the commander obeys. It denies him nothing in the sanctuaries, nothing in the hamlets at night, and nothing against a plan he has read.

**Verdict.** A combined operations command gives the war what it lacked from the first day: one plan and one commander for the war against the regiments, with authority over the ARVN instead of influence on it. Its gains are speed and seams. An ARVN division can be committed in a day or two instead of after days of persuasion. An ARVN battalion calls American fire through a combined centre instead of an adviser's radio. The boundaries between Vietnamese, American and Korean sectors stop being the places a regiment slips through. Those gains are real and moderate: several points on the ability to hold an enemy once found, and more on what an adviser's report can change. They come at three prices. The command will leak, because every plan is Vietnamese-held from its first draft. Every coup will reopen it. And it hands Hanoi the "puppet army" line with a fact attached. Its deepest cost is the one the air-war study warns of: an ARVN that plans and fights inside a combined American staff learns to depend on it, and the staff leaves with the Americans unless it has been run as a school. It does nothing for the war in the hamlets and nothing about the sanctuaries. Whether it moves the war depends on what the ARVN corps commanders do with an order they cannot refuse in form but can still delay in practice.

**Pushes:** ADVISE.leverage +3..+6 (medium), ARVN.effectiveness.fire_coordination +2..+5 (medium), ARVN.effectiveness.combined_arms +1..+3 (low), FIX.capability +2..+4 (medium), INTL.allied_forces +1..+3 (medium), GVN.political_stability -3..+2 (low), POP.gvn_legitimacy -3..+0 (low), ARVN.self_sufficiency.fire_support -4..+0 (medium), INTEL.penetration +1..+3 (low), ENEMY.engagement_control -3..-1 (low) · **Depends on:** ARVN.leadership, GVN.political_stability, US.political_tolerance, STRIKE.responsiveness, LOG.helicopter_hours, ADVISE.leverage, INTL.allied_forces, FIND.main_force

## P012b · Combined Joint Interagency Task Force against the Viet Cong Infrastructure: a standing combined task force on the 2026 counter-network model of the campaigns against al-Qaeda in Iraq, the Taliban and the Islamic State, fusing the intelligence and the assets of civil, military and intelligence agencies of the United States, the Republic of Vietnam, the Republic of Korea and Australia in an F3EAD targeting cycle, with its own exploitation and analysis centre, dedicated lift and ISR, police-led arrest teams and military raid forces for the dismantling of the VC infrastructure, under the GVN's existing arrest and detention law
One combined task force of about 2,500–3,000 people with a national fusion centre in Saigon, four corps-area task groups and a cell in each province [U: the user's default]; police-based and military-based action against the VCI combining civil, military and intelligence agencies [U] · spaces ~900–1,200 US personnel, of whom ~650–900 military spaces [E: about 35–40% of the task force American: analysts, exploitation and SIGINT teams, SOF raid elements, aviation and ISR detachments, liaison to the Agency]; no troop ceiling is set (CONFIG) · arrives 1964-01-01 · FIND, FIX, STRIKE, SUBVERT, SECURE · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Strength ~2,500–3,000 [U]: ~900–1,200 American (~650–900 military), ~1,200–1,500 Vietnamese, ~200–300 Korean, ~100–150 Australian [E: D2]
- Organisation: National Fusion Centre ~400–500; four corps task groups ~350–450 each; 44 province cells ~600–800 total; raid and arrest forces ~1,000–1,200; ~20–30 dedicated helicopters [E: D1]
- Raid tempo: ~30–60 operations a month in early 1964, ~150–250 by end 1965, ~300–450 at maturity in 1966–67; ~60–70% police arrests on warrant [E: D5]
- Yield at maturity: ~300–700 infrastructure members taken a month, ~20–35% district level or above [E: D5]
- Cycle: capture to follow-on target ~6–24 hours, against weeks historically [E: D5]
- Model: TF 714, 18 raids in August 2004, 300 in August 2006 [M012·S10]; effort moved to exploit and analyse [M012·S9]; raids "never sufficient in and of themselves" [M012·S10]
- Historical Phoenix: 81,740 neutralised 1968–72, 26,369 killed, ~87% of the killed in conventional operations [M012·S11]; PRUs ≤4,500 men, 14% of VCI killed [M012·S12]
- Law: 1964 police statute, magistrate review within 72 hours, detention capped at two years, three sources per target [M002]; no new authority [U]
- Cost: ~$60–110 million a year [E: 1964 prices]

**Negative specification.** - **It does not find the main force.** It targets the infrastructure inside the population; it does nothing against a PAVN or VC regiment (A6).
- **It is not TF 714's speed.** It has the method and the organisation, not the drones, the signals or the telephones. Its exploitation runs on paper, interrogation and helicopters. Its cycle is hours to days, not minutes.
- **It brings no new law.** It works under the 1964 police statute: magistrate review within 72 hours, detention capped at two years, three sources per target [M002]. It has no extrajudicial authority.
- **It does not hold the hamlet.** A raid in the contested belt takes one cadre, and his replacement arrives next week unless someone stays.
- **It does not solve detention.** It raises the arrest rate into the prisons and courts that memorandum 006 found were already the binding constraint.
- **It does not replace the district centres or the Special Branch.** It sits on their files, and without them it has nothing to fuse.
- **It does not stop regeneration.** The infrastructure's cadres are replaced from the North, the sanctuaries and the cadre schools; replacement rate, not arrest rate, is the measure.
- **It does not protect itself from capture.** Its national file and its raid arm are the most dangerous instruments in the country in the hands of a president or a junta.
- **It does not make its partners share.** It puts the Special Branch, the MSS and the Agency in one room; it does not make them hand over their best sources.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the infrastructure the province line. A district committee that moves across a provincial boundary has historically escaped one file for another, and here it moves into the same national file. It denies the upper layer its distance: the province and region committee members whom no hamlet policeman ever reached are now targets that a helicopter and a warrant can reach in a night. It denies a captured cadre's network the weeks it used to have to scatter before his papers were read. It denies nothing in the Front's villages, where it can only raid on thin files, and nothing against the main force.

**Verdict.** This task force is the finishing arm the record's war against the infrastructure has lacked. Memorandum 002 gave the war a police that knows the hamlet. Memorandum 006 gave it a method and a centre in every district. This provision gives it a national file across four nations' agencies, a cycle measured in hours, and lift, raiders and arrest teams that can reach a province committee member the same night his name surfaces. Its strongest effect is on the upper layer of the infrastructure, the men who make the hamlet cells into a government, and in the held belt it should take them faster than the Front can train their successors. That is a real and substantial blow to the infrastructure. It is worth stating at full weight, because it is the half of the war the conventional force cannot touch. It is not a transformation, for three reasons the 2026 experience confirms. The record already names most of the infrastructure, so the task force's gain is in finishing rather than finding. Raids alone never defeat a network: they degrade it to an irreducible minimum that holds only where someone holds the ground. And the task force loads the prisons and courts, which were already the binding constraint. Its dangers are penetration, the wrong man in the contested belt, and capture by the palace. Where night security holds, it is the best instrument the war against the infrastructure has. Where it does not, it is the historical Phoenix with better equipment.

# Card 002 — National Police reform with a rural constabulary, and merit-based selection of province and district chiefs

*Memorandum 002 · status complete · full record: memos/002/ · generated by fie.py*

## P002a · National Police Reform Programme, 1964: a resident rural constabulary with a police post in every village, a rebuilt Police Special Branch with sole charge of intelligence on the VC infrastructure, a Police Field Force raised two years early, a national identity and family census, a police pay and career statute, and judicial safeguards on arrest and detention
One national programme: the National Police grown from about 19,000–22,000 in January 1964 to about 70,000 by the end of 1966 and about 95,000 by the end of 1968, of whom about 24,000 rural police resident in villages and about 7,500 Special Branch [E: village and district counts of the period, the historical growth to 88,000 by 1970, and training throughput] · spaces ~520 US personnel, of whom ~150 military spaces [E: about 300 USAID Public Safety advisers against the historical 144 of December 1965, about 150 Army military police and CID training-team spaces, about 70 contractor technicians for the identity system]; about 40 British, Malaysian and Australian police advisers outside US spaces · arrives 1964-01-01 · SECURE, FIND, SUBVERT · institutional

**Key figures.**
- National Police strength: about 19,000–22,000 in January 1964 [M002·S2] [M002·S3]; this provision: about 45,000 by end 1964, about 70,000 by end 1966, about 95,000 by end 1968 [E: training throughput of about 2,500 a month]
- Historical comparison: 53,000 by December 1965 [M002·S3]; 88,000 by 1970 [M002·S2]; 103,859 in February 1971, of whom 27,565 career status [M002·S1]; services extended to the villages only in 1969 [M002·S4]
- Village posts: about 2,400 at full coverage, 8–12 constables each; about 600 manned by end 1964 and 1,500 by end 1965 [E: security-limited occupation]
- Special Branch: about 7,500 by 1966, sole agency for intelligence on the VCI [E: about 15 per district section plus higher staff]
- Police Field Force: about 9,000 by 1966, raised from 1964 rather than January 1966 [E: 44 companies of 150 plus two reserve battalions] [M002·S5]
- Identity and census: about 8 million adults over 15; 400 teams registering about 1.2 million a month in theory; about 60% registered by end 1965 [E: accessible population]
- Cost: about $35–50 million a year running cost at 70,000 men [E: $500–700 per man at 1965 prices]; capital about $60–90 million over three years [E: posts, stations, vehicles, radios, identity system]; US advisory and training about $15–25 million a year [E: about 520 people at full cost]
- US personnel: about 520, of whom about 150 military spaces, against 144 Public Safety advisers historically in December 1965 [M002·S3]
- Safeguards: magistrate review of arrest within 72 hours; detention without trial capped at two years with six-monthly review; three independent sources of evidence for each VCI target [U]

**Negative specification.** - **It does not find the main force.** The police addresses the infrastructure half of find-and-fix and does nothing about a PAVN or VC regiment in a base area (A6).
- **It does not hold a village.** A post of 8–12 constables cannot hold against a VC company; it depends on resident Popular Forces and a reaction that comes at night (POSTNA-2). The police adds knowledge to security; it is not security.
- **It does not work in VC-held villages.** There it works from outside, through informants, prisoners and defectors, and a constable placed in such a village is a hostage.
- **It does not make the police honest by decree.** Pay, an independent paymaster, a discipline board and the Commission Against Corruption reduce predation; they do not end it, and the force's quality follows the honesty of the government that commands it.
- **It is not a larger police than the historical one after 1966.** Its strength roughly matches the historical growth from 1966; its difference is composition, rural presence, the Special Branch and the statute.
- **It does not make an identity card verifiable at a checkpoint.** There is no network in 1964; a card is checked by eye against its photograph, and its fingerprints only at the district station.
- **It does not end the competition among intelligence services.** It orders the army and the Military Security Service to share; their compliance depends on the district chief and the generals.

**Denies the enemy.** Where the government holds a village at night, it denies the VCI anonymity: a stranger is listed nowhere, a cadre's absence is noted, a tax collector who visits is seen by a constable who stays. On the roads and waterways it raises the cost of moving rice, medicine and cash to the enemy. It denies him nothing in the villages he holds, and nothing at all against his main force.

**Verdict.** This is the instrument the theater has lacked for the half of the war that the army cannot fight: a policeman who lives in the village, a Special Branch that knows who the Party's men are, and a register that makes a stranger visible. It is not a larger police than the Republic eventually built, and it does not hold a single village by itself; its value equals the night security beside it, exactly as the land programme's does. Where that security exists, it is the difference between a hamlet the government guards and a hamlet the government knows, and over years that difference is how an insurgency's infrastructure is ground down. Its greatest risks are political: a coup that captures it, a police that preys, and a Special Branch the enemy penetrates. If it survives them, its effect on the infrastructure is substantial and cumulative; it does not touch the main force or the conventional war.

## P002b · Provincial Administration Reform, 1964: merit-based selection of province and district chiefs by an independent Provincial Administration Selection Board, by competitive examination, assessment and vetting, with appointment from a ranked list, a guaranteed two-year tenure removable only for cause, an independent Inspectorate of Provincial Administration, a pay and allowance reform, and a mandatory course before posting
About 290 chief posts (44–45 province chiefs and 239–243 district chiefs) and about 330 deputy posts, filled by competition over 1964–65 [E: the province and district counts of the period, one deputy for administration in each province and district] · spaces ~90 US personnel, of whom ~30 military spaces [E: a small advisory staff to the Selection Board and the Inspectorate, assessment-centre specialists, and province senior advisers' share of the inspection work] · arrives 1964-01-01 · SECURE, ADVISE · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Posts: 44–45 province chiefs and 239–243 district chiefs, about 290 in all [M002·S4] [M002·S12]; about 330 deputies for administration [E: one per province and district, less small districts]; about 620 posts in the system [D]
- Candidate pool: perhaps 900–1,200 credible candidates, officers and civil servants [E: the period's officer corps and the National Institute of Administration's output]
- Selection: written examination, three-day assessment, record review and vetting; appointment from the top three on a published list; refusal of all three only once per vacancy with published reasons [U]
- Tenure: at least two years, normally three; removal only for cause through the Inspectorate, the Commission or court-martial [U]
- Inspectorate: about 120 inspectors in 30 teams of four; every province and district inspected about once a year, with about four unannounced night visits a year per district [E: team-time arithmetic in D5]
- Timeline: first list April 1964; about a third of chiefs replaced in 1964; about two-thirds by mid-1965; nearly all by end 1965 [E: the replacement schedule in D5]
- Cost: about $3–5 million a year, including a pay allowance that roughly doubles the chief's pay [E: period pay scales]
- Historical baseline: Thieu sacked 16 province chiefs by August 1968 and could not find competent replacements [M002·S10]; corrupt province chiefs not removed in January 1968 [M002·S9]
- US personnel: about 90, of whom about 30 military spaces [E: advisory, assessment and inspection staff]

**Negative specification.** - **It does not create competent men.** It selects the best of a thin pool of perhaps 900–1,200 credible candidates for about 620 posts; merit selection cannot select merit that does not exist.
- **It does not survive a coup by itself.** The Board has no force; it survives a coup only if the coup-maker sees more advantage in keeping it, or the American lever is pulled at once.
- **It does not end corruption.** It closes the sale of the post; it does not close the contract, the rice, the draft exemption or the corps commander's business.
- **It does not change the corps commanders.** They still command the divisions and the province chiefs' military operations, and they can obstruct a chief they did not choose.
- **It does not make a chief able to govern a district the enemy holds at night.** Selection needs no security; governing does.
- **It does not make chiefs civilian.** Most remain officers, because the territorial forces must be commanded; civilian chiefs are confined to districts rated secure.
- **It does not act at once.** The first list is published in April 1964; incumbents act until then; full replacement takes until the end of 1965.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy the province chief who works for him by default: the venal, absent or incompetent chief whose Popular Forces sleep in the district town and whose administration drives the population to the Front. It denies him nothing he can win by assassination, which is why competent chiefs become his targets.

**Verdict.** This is the cheapest provision the theater could receive and among the most consequential, because the province and district chief is the government at the level where the war is fought: he commands the territorial forces, directs the police, executes the land reform and decides whether the hamlets are held at night. A chief chosen for ability and kept for two or three years is worth more to a province than any equipment. Its limits are severe and political. It selects from a thin pool, it survives only as long as the junta that keeps it, and its first test, Khanh's coup of 30 January 1964, comes before its first list is published. If the American lever holds it through 1964–65, its effect on provincial administration is substantial and lasting, and it makes every other pacification programme work better. It does not touch the main force or the conventional war.

# Card 006 — Phung Hoang (Phoenix) formalized and modernized from 1964; US unit rotation in place of individual replacement; a selected advisory corps on 18-month tours with 2026 training

*Memorandum 006 · status complete · full record: memos/006/ · generated by fie.py*

## P006a · Phung Hoang (Phoenix) Programme, formalized 1 January 1964 and built to 2026 practice: a national Phung Hoang Committee, Province and District Intelligence and Operations Coordinating Centres (PIOCC and DIOCC) in every province and district, an F3EAD targeting cycle with network analysis and document exploitation, SEEK II-class biometric enrolment of detainees and ralliers, warrant-based targeting under the 1964 police statute, the Provincial Reconnaissance Units raised under that statute, capture-first rules, no quotas, and an independent audit of neutralization claims
One national programme [U]: a national committee and centre, 44 PIOCCs and about 240 DIOCCs at full coverage [E: the period's province and district count], of which about 20 PIOCCs and 100 DIOCCs by end 1964 and all by end 1965 [E: the security-limited occupation of P002a's posts]; about 4,000–5,000 Vietnamese staff in the centres [E: 10–15 per DIOCC, 25–40 per PIOCC, about 150 nationally]; about 1,500 biometric kits [E: one per district station and centre plus field teams] · spaces ~600 US personnel, of whom ~450 military spaces [E: one or two advisers per DIOCC in contested districts, three per PIOCC, a national cell of about 60, an exploitation and analysis detachment of about 80, about 40 biometrics contractors] · arrives 1964-01-01 · FIND, FIX, SUBVERT, SECURE, ADVISE · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Historical Phoenix: ICEX mid-1967, Phung Hoang decree December 1967, ended December 1972; 81,740 neutralized 1968–72, 26,369 killed, about 87% of the killed from conventional operations [M006·S1]
- Centres: national centre ~150 staff, 44 PIOCCs of 25–40, ~240 DIOCCs of 10–15; ~4,000–5,000 Vietnamese staff [E: historical DIOCC manning]
- Build-up: ~100 DIOCCs and 20 PIOCCs by end 1964, all by end 1965 [E: P002a's post occupation]
- PRUs under the police statute from 1964: ~44 units, ~3,000–4,500 men by 1966 [E: historical PRU of ~4,000–5,000 by 1969]
- Throughput: ~2,400–4,800 developed targets a month at full coverage; 30–50% of warrants executed within a month in the held belt, under 10% in the contested belt [E: D5]
- Biometrics: ~1,500 SEEK II kits, offline watchlist up to 120,000 [M006·S3]
- US personnel: ~600, of whom ~450 military spaces [E: D2]
- Cost: ~$15–25 million a year [E: 1964 prices]

**Negative specification.** - **It does not find the main force.** It targets the infrastructure inside the population; it does nothing against a PAVN or VC regiment (A6).
- **It does not work without night security.** In the contested belt it names cadres from ralliers and prisoners and can only raid; raids on thin files kill the wrong men.
- **It is not the 2026 targeting machine.** It keeps the method and loses its inputs: no telephones to exploit, no drones over the hamlet, no data network. The biometric kits work offline against a watchlist of up to 120,000.
- **It is not a new police.** It is a coordinating layer and a method over P002a's Special Branch; without that branch it has nothing to coordinate.
- **It does not make the army share.** The decree puts the army and the Military Security Service in the room; it does not make them hand over their best files.
- **It does not stop the infrastructure regenerating.** Cadres lost in the South are replaced from the North and the sanctuaries; arrest rate is not the measure, replacement rate is.
- **It does not protect itself from capture.** A national file on every suspected cadre is the most valuable instrument a President can seize against his opposition.

**Denies the enemy.** Where night security holds, it denies the infrastructure its upper layer: the district and province committee members whom the hamlet police seldom reach, named from ralliers, prisoners and documents and arrested on warrant from 1965 rather than 1968. It denies the cadre arrested twice under two names his second identity. It denies the Front the propaganda of the historical Phoenix wherever the rules hold. It denies nothing in the villages the Front holds and nothing against the main force.

**Verdict.** In this war Phung Hoang is a coordinating layer and a method placed over a Special Branch that already exists, and its value is the difference between a police that knows the hamlet and one that knows the district committee above it. Where the police posts and the Popular Forces hold at night, it should roughly double the share of senior cadres among those neutralized and do it four years earlier than history, with fewer false arrests, because it has no quotas and its files are built to warrant. Where night security is absent it becomes the historical Phoenix, and its 2026 label will not change that. Its greatest risks are penetration of a fused centre, the press and Congress, and capture by the palace after the Americans leave. It is a real addition to the war against the infrastructure and none at all to the war against the main force.

## P006b · US unit rotation for Southeast Asia: Army and Marine Corps battalions and brigades manned together, stabilised, trained collectively and deployed as units for 12-month tours in place of the individual replacement system, with commanders serving the unit's whole tour, relief in place by whole units with an overlap, battle-loss replacement in trained packets, and the 2026 Army's unit-manning and pre-deployment collective training practice
Applied to every US Army and Marine Corps maneuver battalion and its supporting brigade units deployed to the Republic from 1965 [U]: about 30 battalions in 1965 rising to about 105–110 at the 1968–69 peak [E: the historical deployment of Army and Marine maneuver battalions]; combat support and service units rotate by company and detachment [E: the scale at which they are organised] · spaces ~3–5% above the historical in-country strength on average [E: relief in place with a two- to three-week overlap, about 6% of the year, for each unit once a year]; no new spaces otherwise, and the rotation base in the United States is outside the ceiling · arrives 1964-01-01 · FIX, SECURE, SUSTAIN · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Historical: individual 12-month (Army) and 13-month (Marine) tours; six-month command tours from 1965; no reserve mobilization [M006·S4] [M006·S5]
- Battalions: ~30 maneuver battalions in 1965, ~105–110 at the 1968–69 peak [E: historical deployment]
- Reliefs: ~105–110 a year at the peak, ~2 a week; 2–3 week overlap [E: 2026 practice]
- Extra spaces: ~3–5% average in theater, ~15,000–25,000 at the peak [E: overlap arithmetic]
- Rotation base: ~2 battalions in the cycle at home for each deployed [D]
- Unit cycle: ~4 months individual training, 6–7 months unit training, 12 months deployed within a 24-month draft term [D]
- Losses: 30–50% of riflemen in the heaviest-engaged battalions over a year, refilled by packets of 4–10 [E: period casualty rates]
- 2026 comparison: 9-month BCT tours from 2012, goal of 24 months at home [M006·S6]

**Negative specification.** - **It does not change the tour.** Each man still serves 12 months, and the total number of soldiers needed is about the same [D].
- **It does not keep local knowledge.** A whole battalion arrives new to its area once a year, and a relief in place passes perhaps half of what the outgoing unit knew.
- **It does not survive heavy losses.** A battalion that loses half its riflemen is refilled until it is again a unit of strangers.
- **It does not make bad leaders good.** It keeps commanders for the whole tour, good and bad.
- **It does not stop the late-war breakdown of discipline.** That followed the war's politics and the draft more than the replacement system.
- **It does not fit the draft term easily.** A battalion must deploy within about seven months of forming or its draftees leave before the tour ends.
- **It does not touch the ARVN.** It is an American personnel policy.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy the American unit of strangers with a new commander every six months: the platoon that does not know its own men, the company that forgets its lessons, the ambush sprung by the newest man. It gives him back one thing: a whole battalion new to its area once a year, at a time he can predict.

**Verdict.** Unit rotation trades a constant trickle of strangers for a yearly flood of them. Inside the tour it gives the American battalion stable leaders, collective training before it deploys, and men who know each other, and that should make it fight better at night, in the ambush and under fire, and lose fewer men in its middle months. It costs a few percent more men in theater, a larger formed rotation base without the reserves, and a battalion that knows nothing of its area once a year. The best study of the war doubts that individual rotation was the cause of the late-war breakdown, and this provision will not prevent it. The gain is real and moderate: it improves American units, it does not change which battles the enemy accepts.

**Negative specification.** - **It does not add authority.** The adviser still has no command over his counterpart; longer tours and language deepen influence, not power.
- **It does not create Vietnamese leaders.** Advice changes a commander who will listen, not one who will not.
- **It does not make advisers fluent.** About 24 weeks of Vietnamese gives working conversation, not native ease [E: DLI course lengths].

- **It does not arrive at once.** The first selected advisers reach the field in the second half of 1964; about a third are in post by the end of the first year.
- **It does not end dependence on American fire.** An adviser who can call air and artillery deepens the advised unit's reliance on it unless he is told not to.
- **It does not survive the withdrawal.** It is American and leaves with the Americans.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy the adviser who cannot speak to his counterpart and leaves just as he learns, and the American report that says what the career needs rather than what the adviser saw. It denies him nothing at the regiment level and nothing once the Americans are gone.

**Verdict.** A selected advisory corps on 18-month tours, trained in language and advising to the 2026 standard, is the most direct answer this war can give to the advisory problem the record names: advisers without authority, of falling quality, who leave as they learn. It buys an adviser who is effective for about twelve months instead of six, speaks to his counterpart without an interpreter, and can report honestly. It does not buy authority, it does not make a bad commander good, and it takes good officers from American units. Its effect is a band in advisory leverage, ARVN effectiveness and the territorial forces, and a band against the credibility gap; it is lost when the Americans leave.

**Pushes:** ADVISE.leverage +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], ARVN.effectiveness +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], RFPF.effectiveness +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], US.credibility_gap -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2], US.unit_quality -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2], ARVN.self_sufficiency -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2] · **Depends on:** ARVN.leadership, GVN.political_stability, STRIKE.responsiveness, LOG.helicopter_hours, GVN.corruption, US.personnel_demand

# Card 001 — Accelerated land-to-the-tiller reform and an enforced GVN anti-corruption programme

*Memorandum 001 · status complete · full record: memos/001/ · generated by fie.py*

## P001a · Land-to-the-Tiller Programme, 1964 (accelerated and enhanced): zero retention of tenanted rice land, free distribution to the present tiller, confirmation of Viet Minh and Viet Cong distributions, US-financed landlord compensation, and a fit-for-purpose aerial-photo titling apparatus
One national programme: about 1.0–1.2 million ha of tenanted land to about 850,000–950,000 families [E: Prosterman's 1960–61 tenancy census and the GAO's 1970 LTTT target of 1 million ha to 800,000 tenants] · spaces ~260 US personnel, of whom ~60 military spaces [E: USAID land and survey advisers in each province plus an Army engineer topographic detachment; the 1970s LTTT advisory staff was 31] · arrives 1964-01-01 · SECURE, SUBVERT · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Terms: zero retention of tenanted rice land; owner-cultivators keep up to 15 ha; worship land 5 ha; recipients up to 3 ha (Delta) and 1 ha (Centre); land free; 15-year transfer ban [M001·S2]
- Compensation 2.5 × annual paddy yield, 20% cash and 80% eight-year bonds at 10% [M001·S2], indexed to paddy price in this provision [U]; about $200–280 million at 1964 prices, about 77% US-financed [E: 1970 average of about $282/ha [M001·S3] scaled to 1964]
- Target about 1.0–1.2 million ha to about 850,000–950,000 families [E: Prosterman's census and the GAO's 1970 target]
- Delta 1960–61: 1,175,000 farm families, about 855,000 farming tenanted land; average rent 34% of crop, Centre about 50% [M001·S2]
- Apparatus rate about 40,000–60,000 ha a month if all villages were accessible [E: 120 teams at two villages a team-month]; 1970 programme averaged about 28,000 ha a month [D] (1,007,217 ha in 36 months [M001·S3])
- 1964 titles limited by security to about 15,000–30,000 ha a month, about 150,000–300,000 ha by end-1964 [E: villages accessible by day]
- Rice lands photographed in about three months by two aircraft at 25 cm [D] (from the UltraCam Eagle Mark 3 frame [M001·S10]); no satellite navigation in 1964, so ground control by optical survey [H]
- About 9,000 Vietnamese staff and 260 Americans, of whom about 60 are military spaces [E: organisation in D1–D2]
- Historical comparison: Land to the Tiller (1970) titled 1,198,000 ha with 953,000 titles by end-1973, nearly 40% of cultivated land [M001·S4]

**Negative specification.** It does not make a single hamlet secure at night, and it cannot be delivered in a hamlet the government does not hold: there it is a promise and a registered claim, not a title. It does not stop Viet Cong conscription or coercive taxation, which do not depend on persuasion. It does not reach the main force or Hanoi's will. It does not produce gratitude on any schedule; its effect accrues over seasons and years in what the rural population believes the government's return means. It does not touch the highlands, the plantations or the cities. It is not a guarantee against reversal by the next junta, and it injures the landed families from which much of the officer corps comes. The claim that the 1970 programme cut Viet Cong recruitment by 80% [M001·S11] is the designers' own organisation's claim and is not adopted here. 2026 survey practice that depends on satellite navigation or data networks does not work in 1964; the photography is tied to ground control by optical survey [H].

**Denies the enemy.** The land argument: the claim that the government's return to a hamlet means the landlord's return, and with it the logic that a family must send its sons to the revolution because only the revolution's victory keeps the land [M001·S5]. Where titles are delivered and defended, it denies the infrastructure the consent it taxes by; where they cannot be delivered, it denies the enemy the certainty that the peasant has nothing to gain from the government's arrival.

**Verdict.** This is the provision the theater needs assessment said could touch its first-ranked deficit, and it does: it changes, at a stroke and on paper, the answer to the question that defines the Republic in the countryside, which is what the government's arrival means to a tenant. Six years earlier than history, with the 1970 law's terms and the repairs that law needed, it is a potentially war-shaping political instrument at a negligible cost in money and men. It is not a security measure and it cannot outrun security: in 1964 the government can deliver titles in perhaps a fifth to a half of the Delta's hamlets, and a title in a hamlet the enemy holds at night is a list of targets. Its value therefore depends on what holds the hamlets, on whether the juntas keep it and keep their troops from escorting landlords back, and on whether the officials executing it are honest. Its great virtue is that once a million families have received land, no later government or enemy can easily take that fact back. Its impact on 1964 is modest; its impact on the war, if it survives, is large and slow, and I will say so at full weight.

**Pushes:** POP.land_tenure +3 [old band ≈ +8..+10], POP.gvn_legitimacy +2 [old band ≈ +5..+7], VC.recruitment -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2], VCI.tax_take -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2], POP.rural_economy +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], GVN.political_stability -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2], RFPF.effectiveness +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], ECON.inflation +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], FIND.vci +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], POP.civilian_harm +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], ECON.rice_denial -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2], SUBVERT.defection +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], HANOI.will +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] · **Depends on:** POP.night_control, GVN.admin_capacity, GVN.corruption, GVN.political_stability, GVN.police, RFPF.effectiveness, US.political_tolerance, ADVISE.leverage, LOG.helicopter_hours

## P001b · GVN Anti-Corruption Programme with Enforcement Mechanism: an independent Commission Against Corruption on the Hong Kong ICAC model with powers of arrest, search, seizure and compelled asset declaration, a special anti-corruption court, an independent RVNAF pay-and-muster verification service, and a joint US–GVN Aid Compliance Board empowered to suspend aid to a command or ministry
One national commission of about 2,000 Vietnamese staff with about 320 US advisers, investigators and auditors [E: ICAC's 1,213 staff for a city of about 7 million, scaled for a country of about 15 million and an armed force of about 514,000] · spaces ~320 US personnel, of whom ~140 military spaces [E: Army CID agents, finance and audit officers and muster teams; the rest USAID, Treasury and GAO-trained civilians] · arrives 1964-01-01 · ADVISE, SUSTAIN, SECURE · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Design: independent Commission on the Hong Kong ICAC model (Operations, Corruption Prevention, Community Relations; powers to arrest, search and seize) [M001·S12], a Special Court, a Pay and Muster Verification Service, a joint US–GVN Aid Compliance Board able to suspend aid to a command, importer or province, asset declarations for majors and above, and a limited amnesty for pre-1964 petty corruption [U]
- About 2,000 Vietnamese staff and about 320 Americans, about 140 of them military spaces [E: ICAC's 1,213 staff [M001·S12] scaled for the RVN]
- Musters about 480 units a month, the whole RVNAF of about 514,000 [M001·S24] about twice a year; biometric enrolment complete in about nine months [E: 60 teams and 600 kits]
- About 1,500–2,500 cases opened and 300–500 brought to court a year; the court tries about 300–400 [E: a new commission's caseload]
- Ghost-soldier benchmarks: Iraq 50,000 (2014) [M001·S16]; Afghanistan about 42,000 fewer on biometric validation (2019) [M001·S15]; Afghan pay system with 7,714 records absent from the biometric database [M001·S14]
- If 5–10% of RVNAF rolls are ghosts, about 25,000–50,000 paper spaces exposed [E: no reliable count exists; phantom troops reported in the press in 1965 [M001·S17]]
- The lever: Commercial Import Program obligations of $397 million in 1966 [M001·S21], whose counterpart piasters paid the army, police and civil service [M001·S20]

**Negative specification.** It does not end corruption in the Republic, and it does not reach the junta itself without a patron stronger than the generals it would accuse. It does not make officers competent; it removes some who are corrupt and exposed, and only where a replacement exists. Biometric identity cards do not stop a commander who controls who is enrolled; only the independent, physical muster does that, and only where a team can reach. It does not pay a soldier enough to live on in an inflating economy, so petty corruption born of need survives it. It is not an instrument against the Viet Cong. It is likely to be used by factions against each other. Its enforcement lever, the Aid Compliance Board, is American and cannot be transferred; it weakens as American aid falls, and every suspension costs the Republic part of its claim to be its own government (POSTNA-6).

**Denies the enemy.** One of the Front's strongest themes, a corrupt regime that robs its own soldiers and people, where convictions are visible and reach above the district. Some of the black market through which American goods reach the enemy, and some of the bribes by which his agents buy documents and posts. Above all it denies him the hollow battalion: a unit carried at a strength it does not have, whose commander and whose advisers do not know how weak it is until it breaks.

**Verdict.** This is a smaller provision than it sounds and a more important one than its figures will show. It will not clean the Saigon government, and in a junta that makes coups its most likely failure is to become one faction's weapon against another. What it can do reliably is the physical part: count the army, put the pay in the soldier's hand, and end the ghost battalion, which strengthens the RVNAF's real fighting power, reduces one cause of desertion, and gives this headquarters a true strength return for the first time (G-10). What it may do, if it is protected and the American lever is used and seen to be used, is change what an officer expects to happen to him if he buys a command or sells his men's rice, which reaches the officer corps (G-4) where nothing in an arsenal can. Its greatest value may be to the land programme (P001a), whose officials it watches. Its greatest cost is political: it threatens the incomes of the men who make governments, and it gives the Americans a hand on the Republic's throat that the enemy will name for what it is.

# Card 007 — Officer education to the 2026 standard for new US and ARVN officers from 1957, gating promotion; ARVN officer selection and promotion reform

*Memorandum 007 · status complete · full record: memos/007/ · generated by fie.py*

## P007a · US officer education to the 2026 standard for new officers of the Army and Marine Corps (and the Air Force and Navy continua), commissioned from 1957: the Army's Basic Officer Leader Course (BOLC A and B), Captains Career Course with its distributed-learning phase, and Command and General Staff Officer Course (Intermediate Level Education); the Marine Corps' Basic School, Expeditionary Warfare School and Command and Staff College; each course a gate for the next promotion
Every new US officer commissioned from 1957 [U]: about 15,000–20,000 Army and Marine officers a year in 1957–64, rising to about 40,000–50,000 a year at the 1967–69 peak [E: active Army and Marine officer accessions of the period, with the wartime OCS expansion]; the 1957–63 classes completed it before the campaign opened [U: standing condition officer_cohorts_1957] · spaces ~0 in RVN [E: every course is taught in the United States]; about 1,500–2,500 instructor and staff spaces added to the training base in the United States by 1967, outside the ceiling [E: student load at 2026 small-group ratios]; in effect about 4–6% of the company- and field-grade officer strength in school at any time instead of in units [E: course lengths against career length]; no troop ceiling is set (CONFIG) · arrives 1964-01-01 · ADVISE, FIX, SECURE, SUSTAIN · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Courses: Army BOLC B (branch, ~4–6 months, separation if not done within 2 years of commissioning) [M007·S6]; Captains Career Course with a 75-hour distributed phase [M007·S12]; CGSOC 10 months resident [M007·S8]; USMC TBS ~6 months [E: commonly given], EWS 41 weeks [M007·S10]
- Gates: BOLC B before 1LT, CCC or EWS before MAJ, staff course before LTC [E: 2026 sequence applied as a hard bar per the grant]
- Accessions: ~15,000–20,000 Army and Marine officers a year in 1957–64, ~40,000–50,000 a year at the 1967–69 peak [E: period accessions]
- 1957–63 classes: ~100,000–130,000 commissioned, about two-thirds still serving in 1964 [E: accessions less obligated-service losses]
- First educated battalion commanders: about 1971–72 [E: promotion timing]
- Cost: ~4–6% of company- and field-grade officers in school at any time; ~1,500–2,500 added instructors at the peak; 0 spaces in RVN [E: D2, D8]
- Margin: an educated platoon leader is about as competent in month one as a historical one in months four to six [X-007]

**Negative specification.** - **It does not reach the men who run the war.** Battalion, brigade and division commanders and every general in 1964–70 were commissioned before 1957 and are untouched; the first educated battalion commanders arrive about 1971–72.
- **It is not a counterinsurgency course.** The 2026 curriculum is built first for large-scale combat against a peer; the Iraq and Afghanistan lessons are present but secondary.
- **It does not change the strategy, the body count or the replacement system.** It makes better junior officers inside them; P006b's unit rotation, not this, addresses the replacement system.
- **It does not raise commissioning standards.** It educates officers after they are commissioned; it does not impose the 2026 degree requirement on Officer Candidate School.
- **It costs captains.** At any time about one captain in eight is in school from 1966, and the wartime pipeline for platoon leaders is three to four months longer.
- **It does not teach the hamlet.** Its knowledge of Vietnam comes from Americans who served there, not from the Vietnamese.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy some of the young American officer's mistakes: the platoon walked into a horseshoe ambush on a trail, the company that loses its fire support plan in the first minutes of contact, the lieutenant who cannot read the map in the canopy. It denies him nothing at the operational level.

**Verdict.** This is a modest provision for the American side of the war and a real one. It makes the platoon leaders and company commanders of 1964–70 markedly better at their work, which saves American lives at the margin and some Vietnamese civilian lives where the lieutenant's discipline over fire and detainees holds. It does not touch the men who decide how the war is fought until the war is nearly over, and it is built for a different war from the one of 1964–65. Its largest value may be indirect: as the faculty and the common language for its ARVN counterpart, and as the education of the advisers who remain when the American units leave.

**Pushes:** US.unit_quality +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], US.casualties -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2], POP.civilian_harm -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2], US.personnel_demand +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] · **Depends on:** US.political_tolerance, US.unit_quality, US.personnel_demand

- Historical schooling: field-grade command and staff schools only from 1967; ninth-grade diploma required for major; most officers without formal training in 1969 [M007·S1]
- Commissions under the provision: ~2,000–3,000 a year in 1957–63, ~4,000–6,000 in 1964–67, ~8,000–12,000 at the 1968–71 peak [E: S2 and S3 averages and the mobilization]
- 1957–63 classes: ~13,000–18,000 commissioned, ~10,000–14,000 serving on 1 Jan 1964 [E: same]
- Gates: branch basic course (~4–5 months) before 1LT, career course (~5–6 months) before MAJ, Dalat staff course (~9–10 months) before LTC [U] [E: US models]
- US spaces: ~300–450 military of ~350–500 US personnel [E: faculty advisers]; Vietnamese instructors ~600–1,800 added [E: 2026 ratios]
- Battalion commanders with full education: ~1 in 5 historically, ~4 in 5 by 1967 [X-007]
- Officers in school at any time: ~5–8% of company- and field-grade [E: course lengths]

**Negative specification.** - **It does not reach the generals.** Corps and division commanders and the juntas of 1964–70 were commissioned before 1957; command at the top stays a political appointment until P007c reaches it.
- **It does not choose commanders.** It makes officers eligible; it does not put them in command. Without P007c the educated captain can be passed over for a loyalist.
- **It does not pay officers.** An educated captain whose salary has lost its value to inflation is as corruptible as an uneducated one.
- **It does not teach night security by itself.** The territorial war is learned by living in it; the course gives the vocabulary, not the trust of a hamlet.
- **It costs majors.** The career-course gate slows the making of majors in the grade the army was shortest of; only the 1957–63 classes, already through it, cover the gap in 1964–67.
- **It does not keep officers out of politics.** An educated officer corps with blocked promotion is a coup faction.
- **It deepens the habit of American fire support.** Common doctrine makes combined operations easier and the dependence on American fire deeper.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy the ARVN battalion that walks down the road into the ambush the regiment laid for it: the incompetent company commander, the fire plan never made, the relief column that does not scout its route. It denies him some of the ARVN's tactical predictability, which the enemy's regiments exploited from Binh Gia onwards. It does not deny him the political general who orders the battalion to stand still.

**Verdict.** This is a substantial provision. With the 1957–63 classes in place, the ARVN's company-grade officers in 1964 are educated to a standard the historical army never reached, and from 1965 the battalions are commanded by them. That attacks the ARVN's most cited weakness — poor leadership, which American advisers named as the foremost reason for ineffective units — from below, and it does so in the years the war was lost in the countryside. Its ceiling is set above it: education does not choose commanders, pay officers or govern the generals. It makes P007c possible, because a merit system needs a pool of qualified officers to choose from, and it enlarges the small pool of able field-grade officers the record says every reform drew on. Alone it is a +1 to ARVN effectiveness; with a selection system that uses it, much more.

**Pushes:** ARVN.leadership +2 [old band ≈ +5..+7], ARVN.effectiveness +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], ARVN.self_sufficiency +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], RFPF.effectiveness +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], ADVISE.leverage +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] · **Depends on:** ARVN.leadership, ADVISE.leverage, GVN.political_stability, GVN.corruption

## P007c · RVNAF Officer Selection and Promotion Reform, 1964: an independent Officer Selection and Promotion Board under the Joint General Staff with written criteria, a two-tier rater and senior-rater evaluation report on the 2026 US model with a capped top block, centrally selected battalion and regimental command lists, relief for cause, an open path to commission for proven NCOs, removal of the diploma bar to promotion, and general-officer promotion and division command filled from a ranked board list, protected by an American aid condition
One national board system [U]: about 12,000–16,000 officer promotions and about 150–250 battalion and regimental command selections a year in 1964–67 [E: an officer corps of about 18,000–24,000 regular officers in 1964 growing toward 50,000–60,000 by 1972, with the 1969 increment of 2,653 senior officers per S1] · spaces ~60–90 US personnel, of whom ~40–60 military spaces [E: an advisory cell to the board and the JGS personnel directorate, evaluation-system trainers, and a share of the senior advisers' time]; no troop ceiling is set (CONFIG) · arrives 1964-01-01 · ADVISE, SECURE · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Historical: Diem's President chose from a confidential list [M007·S4]; corps and division commanders appointed for loyalty [M007·S5]; ninth-grade diploma for major; 80 of 133 battalion commanders in command a year or less in May 1971; 46 of 133 battalions captain-led [M007·S1]
- Board: ~200–350 Vietnamese staff; ~40–80 senior officers on panels [E: design]
- Throughput: ~12,000–16,000 promotions and ~150–250 command selections a year in 1964–67 [E: officer corps of ~18,000–24,000 regulars in 1964]
- Command tour: fixed 18–24 months [E: design]
- OER: senior-rater top block capped at about a third [E: 2026 US model]
- General officers: President chooses from a board's ranked list of three, enforced by an aid condition [E: design]
- US personnel: ~60–90, of whom ~40–60 military [E: design]
- Margin: competent battalion commanders ~1/2 historically to ~3/4 by 1967; median command tour under 1 year to ~18 months; 1–2 division commands in 10 changed by 1967 [X-007]

**Negative specification.** - **It does not take command of divisions and corps out of politics.** The President still appoints generals, from a ranked list of three; the aid condition can enforce the list, not the choice.
- **It does not stop coups.** A coup is a promotion list written by force; the reform raises its price and raises the risk of one while it beds in.
- **It does not create able officers.** It chooses among those that exist; its pool is P007b's educated classes and the small pool of able field-grade officers the record says every reform already draws on.
- **It does not see loyalty or penetration.** The board reads performance, not a man's faction, his patrons, or his contact with the enemy.
- **It does not work without the American lever,** and the lever weakens after 1969 and is gone after 1973.
- **It does not end corruption.** It makes the sale of commands harder and visible; it does not raise pay.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy the ARVN battalion led by a commander who bought his command, holds it for six months and is never relieved; and, slowly, the division led by a general chosen because he would never move against the palace. It denies the enemy part of the predictability he exploited — the commander who would not close with the enemy because his career depended on avoiding losses.

**Verdict.** This is the provision that decides whether the education is used. Below the generals it works: battalions get chosen commanders who serve full tours and are relieved when they fail, and educated officers rise. At the top it is as strong as the American will to enforce a list, and no stronger; the junta years of 1964–65 will test it at once. It is the first serious answer in this war to the gap in the officer corps that the record holds open, and it is the reform most likely to provoke the generals it threatens. I judge it worth that risk. Its effect is institutional and accrues over years: it will show in battalion outcomes from 1966 and in the divisions only if the lever holds.

**Pushes:** ARVN.leadership +2 [old band ≈ +5..+7], ARVN.effectiveness +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], GVN.corruption -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2], ARVN.desertion -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2], GVN.political_stability -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2] · **Depends on:** ADVISE.leverage, GVN.political_stability, GVN.admin_capacity, INTEL.penetration, GVN.corruption, US.political_tolerance

## Employment concepts
EC007-1 the gate and the branch course · EC007-2 the Dalat staff year · EC007-3 the board season · EC007-4 relief for cause and the thirty-day review · EC007-5 the field commission · EC007-6 the platoon leader's first month (with P006b) · EC007-7 the career course to the advisory corps (with P006c). Abandoned: EC007-8 the adviser's rating (adviser becomes a superior; proof of American selection) · EC007-9 promotion on the scoreboard (rewards inflated body counts) · EC007-10 Leavenworth for all (capacity, language, the American label) · EC007-11 the wartime waiver (sold within a season; replaced by one deferral)

## Interactions
- P007b × P007c: education makes an officer eligible and the board decides whether he commands; each is worth a fraction of the pair, and together they give the ARVN its first pipeline that produces and rewards able officers (F007-1)
- P007b, P007c × P002b: the educated classes enlarge the pool the province list draws on from 1966; the evaluation reports give the Selection Board a record of each officer's field performance; in 1964–65 the two boards still compete for the same few field-grade men (F007-2)
- P007b × P006c: the selected adviser advises a counterpart educated on the same curriculum; the argument moves from teaching doctrine to applying it, and the adviser's Vietnamese reaches a counterpart who has the vocabulary to answer (F007-3)
- P007a × P006c: the Captains Career Course is the pipeline of the selected advisory corps; the advisers of 1966–70 are career-course graduates, and the course and the corps compete for the same captains (F007-11)
- P007a × P006b: the educated lieutenant joins a battalion that trains collectively for six to seven months before it deploys and keeps him for the whole tour; the platoon leader and the platoon learn together, once
- P007c × P001b: the Commission is the board's enforcement arm against sold promotions and commands, and the Aid Compliance Board carries the aid condition that protects the general-officer list; the evaluation report gives the Commission a paper trail it never had
- P007b, P007c × P004a, P004b, P004c: an educated company commander employs the marksman as an overwatch and the squad gun as a base of fire because both are in his course; battalion sniper pools and volume-of-fire doctrine, which 004 recorded as abandoned, are not tried by officers taught why they fail
- P007c × P006a: army officers posted to the district centres are rated, and their reports are a target; the board's files and the Phung Hoang file are two lists of loyalties in two buildings, and the enemy wants both (F007-6)
- P007b × P005c, P003b: the company commander educated to call fire uses the American fire the adviser brings more effectively, and depends on it more (F007-23)

- P002a (memo 002) pushes +3 [old band ≈ +8..+10] — A resident constable in each village that the government holds, a district station in every district, and a police force paid enough not to live on the population: the National Police becomes a rural institution five years before it did historically
- P002b (memo 002) depends — A district chief governs through the police as well as the Popular Forces (P002a)
- P006a (memo 006) depends — Phung Hoang is a coordinating layer over P002a's Special Branch; without it there is nothing to coordinate

### GVN.political_stability
- P001a (memo 001) pushes -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2] — Expropriates the landed class from which much of the officer corps and the civil service come; a coup grievance in a junta already prone to coups
- P001b (memo 001) pushes -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2] — Threatens the incomes of the generals who make and unmake governments; prosecutions become coup grievances and coup weapons
- P001a (memo 001) depends — The decree must survive the next coup; each new junta may reopen it
- P001b (memo 001) depends — The commission lives only while some faction in Saigon protects it
- P002a (memo 002) pushes +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] — A Special Branch that watches the generals as well as the VC, and a police that is not one faction's instrument, slightly raises the cost of a coup; the reform is itself a prize for the faction that captures it
- P002b (memo 002) pushes -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2] — Takes from the generals their most valuable patronage; a coup grievance in 1964, and a coup-maker's first target is the selection board
- P002a (memo 002) depends — Every junta since 1955 has used the police as a political instrument; the Director General's fixed term survives only while a coup does not sweep it away
- P002b (memo 002) depends — The Board and the two-year tenure survive only as long as the government that decreed them, and the next coup may sweep both
- P006a (memo 006) depends — Each coup changes the committee's chairman and tempts its use against the opposition
- P006c (memo 006) depends — Counterparts appointed and removed by coup outlast no adviser
- P007c (memo 007) pushes -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2] — The reform takes the junta's main currency, which raises the coup risk while it beds in
- P007b (memo 007) depends — Coups make the promotion list and override the gate
- P007c (memo 007) depends — A junta can suspend the board; a coup is a promotion list
- P008a (memo 008) depends — State enterprises and licences change hands with each government
- P011a (memo 011) pushes +0..+2 (low) — Thieu's government keeps faith longer in the assurances it was given; the panic of 1975 starts from a firmer belief that Washington will act

### INTEL.penetration
- P001b (memo 001) pushes -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2] — Investigations of officials who sell documents, passes and posts uncover some of the enemy's purchased agents
- P001b (memo 001) depends — A commission holding the regime's secrets is a target for the enemy's agents as well as the generals'
- P002a (memo 002) pushes -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2] — Special Branch counter-intelligence and vetting against an enemy that has had agents in the police and the RVNAF for a decade; partial, and itself a target
- P002a (memo 002) depends — A Special Branch penetrated by the enemy hands him its informants
- P003a (memo 003) depends — Anything shared with the Joint General Staff can reach the enemy; the product is only as secret as the least secure office that reads it
- P005a (memo 005) depends — B-52 strikes in the South need GVN clearance; a penetrated clearance chain warns the target whatever the bomb
- P006a (memo 006) depends — A fused file in a penetrated centre is the enemy's list of our informants
- P007c (memo 007) depends — Board files and command lists are a target for enemy agents in the JGS
- P008b (memo 008) depends — Plant workforces and signal depots are open to agents

No earlier contributions.

- P001a (memo 001) depends — Land teams and survey parties reach contested villages by air
- P002a (memo 002) depends — Field Force companies and identity teams reach villages off the roads by air
- P003b (memo 003) depends — The reaction to a radar track in the South is an airmobile force; in 1964 there are few helicopter hours to spend on it
- P006c (memo 006) depends — Medevac and resupply for the advised unit come through the adviser
- P009a (memo 009) depends — The tourniquet buys the wounded man an hour or two; the Dustoff and the surgical bed decide whether he uses it
- P009b (memo 009) depends — The RVNAF's wounded waited longer for evacuation than the American; the tourniquet's value rises with the wait and its cost in limbs rises with it

### POP.civilian_harm
- P001a (memo 001) pushes +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] — Titled families and land committee members in contested hamlets become targets of the enemy's security sections (F001-8)
- P002a (memo 002) pushes -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2] — Arrest on evidence and detention under review replace part of the military's sweep-and-detain; offset in part by enemy terror against resident constables
- P003b (memo 003) pushes +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] — Night movement tracks in the Delta and the coastal plain are fired on under the historical rules; a radar cannot tell a farmer's sampan from a VC supply sampan
- P005b (memo 005) pushes -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2] — Point targets no longer need area boxes; offset by more targets struck
- P005c (memo 005) pushes -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2] — Smaller bombs on single aimpoints instead of a carpet of 108
- P006a (memo 006) pushes -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2] — Warrants, capture-first rules and no quotas against the historical Phoenix of feud and quota; the PRUs remain the risk
- P007a (memo 007) pushes -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2] — Law of war, the Army profession and escalation-of-force training reach every new platoon leader, including the wartime OCS classes
- P009c (memo 009) pushes -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2] — Fire discipline and the conduct block reach the hamlet militia, whose conduct toward the population was the GVN's face in the countryside; small
- P010a (memo 010) pushes -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2] — The squad leader is the man who controls fire in the hamlet and the detainee at the trail; small
- P011c (memo 011) pushes -1 (high) — 347–504 villagers of Son My live; a trace against the civilian dead of the whole war, which is the honest weight
